title: How to Keep Client Data Safe When Your Team Uses AI Tools
dek: Keep client data safe with AI tools: what never goes into a free chatbot, how business plans handle training, and a one-page policy your team will follow.
keywords: keep client data safe AI tools
AI tools data policy for agencies
does ChatGPT train on my data
business vs free AI plans data training
AI acceptable use policy small business
summary: You keep client data safe with AI tools by approving specific tools in writing, using business plans that exclude your data from training by default, and keeping real client details out of personal accounts. A person then reviews anything client-facing before it goes out. Most exposure comes from everyday habits, not hackers.

hero.alt: A 1930s pulp noir illustration of Momo the robot mascot as a night watchman holding a lantern, standing guard before a large bank vault door

takeaways: The biggest client data risk with AI tools is a team member pasting real client details into a personal account, not a break-in.
OpenAI says ChatGPT Business workspace data is excluded from model training by default.
Anthropic says its commercial products, including Claude for Work and its API, do not train on your inputs by default, while consumer plans let each user choose.
A one-page list of approved tools and banned data types prevents more problems than any single setting.
Every AI draft that touches client information should be read by a person who knows the account before it leaves the building.

body.heading: What client data is at risk when your team uses AI tools?
paragraphs: Any information a client shared expecting it to stay private is at risk the moment it is typed into the wrong tool. That covers far more than names and email addresses.

subsections.heading: The obvious data
paragraphs: Customer lists, contact details, contracts, invoices and login details are the clear cases. Most teams already know these are sensitive, yet they still end up in chats when someone is rushing.

subsections.heading: The data people forget
paragraphs: Unreleased campaigns, ad account exports, internal sales numbers, call recordings and meeting notes are just as private. A pasted spreadsheet of ad results can carry customer emails or revenue figures nobody meant to share.

subsections.heading: How the leak actually happens
paragraphs: The usual risk is not a hacker. It is a busy team member pasting a client file into a personal AI account to save ten minutes, without knowing how that account handles the input.
The right account type and a short written policy remove most of that risk. The rest comes down to habits, which a few minutes of training can fix.

body.heading: How do AI tools use the data you type in?
paragraphs: It depends on the plan, not just the company. The same AI provider often treats consumer accounts and business accounts very differently, so the plan your team logs into is the detail that matters.

subsections.heading: Consumer plans
paragraphs: Free and personal paid plans often let the provider use chats to improve its models unless the user changes a setting. Anthropic, for example, [updated its consumer terms](https://www.anthropic.com/news/updates-to-our-consumer-terms) so that users on Claude Free, Pro and Max choose whether their chats can be used for training, with data kept up to five years if they opt in and 30 days if they do not.

subsections.heading: Business plans
paragraphs: Business and enterprise plans usually exclude your data from training by default. OpenAI says [ChatGPT Business workspace data](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/8798634-how-your-data-is-used-to-improve-model-performance) is excluded from training by default and encrypted in transit and at rest, and Anthropic says its [commercial products](https://privacy.anthropic.com/en/articles/7996868-is-my-data-used-for-model-training) such as Claude for Work and its API do not train on inputs or outputs by default.
Business plans also tend to add admin controls, so an owner can see who has access and remove people. Those controls matter as much as the training setting.

subsections.heading: Feedback buttons
paragraphs: Thumbs up and thumbs down buttons can change the rules for that chat. Anthropic says that when you send feedback this way it may store the whole related conversation for up to five years and use it to train models, even on commercial plans.

body.heading: What should never go into a free AI tool?
paragraphs: Anything you would not post on a public forum should stay out of a free or personal AI account. If a client would be upset to learn it left your systems, it does not go in.

That rule covers customer lists, financial figures, passwords and API keys, contracts, unreleased creative, health or legal details and anything under a signed confidentiality agreement. Free tools are still fine for general research, brainstorming and drafts that use placeholder details like Client A and 100 sample leads.
This is not a ban on AI. It is a rule that the tool has to earn trust first, with clear answers on training, retention and who can see the data.
Put these rules into a one-page policy that names the approved tools, the banned data types and who to ask when unsure. Share it with everyone who touches client accounts, contractors included.

body.heading: How do you check whether an AI tool is safe for client work?
paragraphs: Check the plan's data terms before anyone uses it for client work, not after. Five questions cover most of what matters.

Step 1: Find the plan's privacy or data page and look for whether inputs are used to train models by default. Write down the exact plan name, because the answer often changes between free and business tiers.
Step 2: Check how long the provider keeps your data and whether an admin can change it. Shorter retention means less sitting on someone else's servers.
Step 3: Confirm the plan has an admin console, single sign on or at least a way to remove a user the day they leave. Access you cannot revoke is access you cannot control.
Step 4: Look at what connectors and integrations the tool can reach, like Google Drive or your inbox. A tool that can read a shared drive can read every client folder in it.
Step 5: If any answer is unclear, email the vendor and keep the reply. A vendor that cannot explain where your data goes has answered the question for you.
Step 6: Write the result into your approved tools list with the date you checked. When the vendor changes its terms later, you will know exactly what changed.

body.heading: What does a safe day-to-day setup look like?
paragraphs: A safe setup keeps each client separate, keeps client work on business accounts and keeps a person in the loop before anything goes out. None of it slows a good team down.

subsections.heading: Separate spaces per client
paragraphs: Each client's files, prompts and outputs live in their own project or folder, open only to the people on that account. Pooling everything into one shared space is how one client's details end up in another's draft.

The same goes for AI agents that run routine tasks. Give each one access to a single client's folder, the way we describe in [a day in the life of an AI marketing agent](/daily/ai-marketing-agents-day-in-the-life).

subsections.heading: Business accounts only for client work
paragraphs: Client work happens on approved business accounts with training off by default. Personal accounts stay for personal tasks.

subsections.heading: A person reviews before anything ships
paragraphs: Every AI draft that touches client information gets read by someone who knows the account before it goes to the client or a live campaign. We explain how that works in [why AI agents need human approval](/daily/human-approval-ai-agents) and [how AI agents hand work to people](/daily/how-ai-agents-hand-work-to-people).

subsections.heading: Placeholders in prompts
paragraphs: When a task does not need the real details, swap them out before you paste. Client A and Product X work just as well for an outline, and the real names go back in later on an approved account.

subsections.heading: Clean offboarding
paragraphs: When someone leaves, remove their access to every AI tool on the same day you close their email. Old accounts are the access most teams forget.
Keep a simple list of which people have which AI accounts. It turns offboarding into a five minute checklist instead of a guess.

body.heading: A simple worked example: a six-person team
paragraphs: Here is an example with made-up numbers, not a statistic. A six-person team where each person pastes client details into a personal AI account about 3 times a week creates 18 uncontrolled uses a week.
Over a year, that is 18 times 52, or 936 times client data went somewhere the business never reviewed. Spread across 12 months, it is about 78 a month.

Move the same work to one approved business workspace with training off by default, and the count of uncontrolled uses drops toward zero without anyone working slower. The time cost is one afternoon to set up the workspace and one page of rules.
The exact count is not the point. The example shows how small daily shortcuts add up to a large exposure that no one ever decided to accept.

body.heading: What are the most common mistakes teams make?
paragraphs: The most common mistake is assuming a paid plan is automatically a business plan. A personal paid subscription is often still a consumer plan with consumer data terms.

subsections.heading: Trusting the default without reading it
paragraphs: Defaults change, and they differ by plan. Read the setting on the account your team actually uses.

subsections.heading: Checking once and never again
paragraphs: Providers update their terms, sometimes in ways that matter for client work. Review your approved list at least twice a year, and put the review on the calendar so it does not depend on memory.

subsections.heading: Connecting everything
paragraphs: Giving an AI tool access to your whole drive or inbox exposes every client at once. Connect only the folders a task needs.

subsections.heading: Forgetting meeting tools
paragraphs: AI note takers and transcription tools capture everything said on a call, including client details. Put them through the same check as any other AI tool or keep them off client calls.

subsections.heading: No written rules
paragraphs: If the rules live in one person's head, everyone else guesses. A one-page policy shared with everyone who touches client accounts fixes that.

body.heading: Do you need an enterprise AI plan for client work?
paragraphs: Not always, but you do need a business-grade plan for anything that touches real client data. The right tier depends on your size and what your contracts require.

subsections.heading: A business or enterprise plan makes sense if
paragraphs: Your team handles client files, customer lists or ad account data, or your client contracts include confidentiality or data handling terms. It also makes sense once more than one or two people use AI daily, because admin controls and offboarding start to matter.

subsections.heading: Free or personal tools are fine if
paragraphs: The work involves no real client details, such as general research, outlines or drafts with placeholders. If you are unsure where AI fits at all, start with our guide to [AI agents vs chatbots](/daily/ai-agents-vs-chatbots) and decide what jobs you actually need help with.

subsections.heading: Ask your clients too
paragraphs: Some clients set their own AI rules in contracts or vendor policies. Ask before you start and save their answer in that client's folder.

faq.question: Can I use free AI tools for client work at all?
faq.answer: Only for work with no real client details, such as research, brainstorming or drafts with placeholder names. Anything with real client information belongs on an approved business account.

faq.question: Does ChatGPT train on my team's data?
faq.answer: It depends on the plan. OpenAI says ChatGPT Business workspace data is excluded from training by default, while personal accounts have their own data controls that each user must check.

faq.question: Is a personal paid AI subscription safe for client data?
faq.answer: Not automatically. Many personal paid plans fall under consumer terms, so check the training and retention settings for that exact plan before using it for client work.

faq.question: Can clicking thumbs up or down share my conversation?
faq.answer: It can. Anthropic, for example, says feedback sent this way may store the whole related conversation for up to five years and use it for training, even on commercial plans.

faq.question: How often should we review our approved AI tools?
faq.answer: At least twice a year and whenever a provider announces new terms. Policies change more often than most teams check.
